reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A rare, largely benign lymphoproliferative interstitial process classified among the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias but usually secondary to an underlying disorder.
Strongly associated with Sjögren syndrome, other connective tissue diseases, HIV infection (especially in children), common variable immunodeficiency and autoimmune thyroid disease.
Presents insidiously with cough and breathlessness, sometimes with systemic or autoimmune features.
The HRCT hallmark is diffuse ground-glass opacity with scattered thin-walled perivascular cysts; centrilobular nodules and septal thickening are also seen.
Histology shows a dense polyclonal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate expanding the alveolar septa.
It must be distinguished from pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, and clonality studies may be required.
Disease often responds to corticosteroids and to treatment of the underlying disorder.
Always undertake an immunodeficiency and autoimmune work-up, including immunoglobulins and HIV testing.
reference.pathophysiology: LIP represents a reactive, polyclonal proliferation of lymphocytes and plasma cells that diffusely infiltrate the pulmonary interstitium and alveolar septa, frequently driven by autoimmune states (notably Sjögren syndrome), immunodeficiency and chronic antigenic or viral stimulation. Peribronchiolar lymphoid infiltration with air trapping is thought to produce the characteristic thin-walled cysts.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary MALT lymphoma and other lymphoproliferative disease
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis or Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome as cystic mimics
Pneumocystis or other opportunistic infection in the immunocompromised
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax to characterise ground-glass change and cysts
Autoimmune serology and a Sjögren work-up including anti-Ro/La antibodies and Schirmer test
HIV testing and serum immunoglobulins with electrophoresis
Surgical lung biopsy with immunohistochemistry and clonality studies to exclude lymphoma
Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor
redFlags: Rapid enlargement of nodules or masses suggesting transformation to lymphoma
Constitutional symptoms raising concern for malignancy
New opportunistic infection in an immunocompromised patient
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; many patients stabilise or improve with treatment of the underlying disorder, but some progress to fibrosis or, uncommonly, transform to lymphoma.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing low-grade pulmonary lymphoma as LIP or vice versa
Failing to investigate for Sjögren syndrome, HIV or immunodeficiency
Attributing pulmonary cysts solely to lymphangioleiomyomatosis or emphysema
Assuming a purely idiopathic process without searching for a secondary cause
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
ATS/ERS international multidisciplinary classification of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
management: Treat the underlying disorder, with antiretroviral therapy in HIV, immunoglobulin replacement in common variable immunodeficiency, and control of Sjogren syndrome or other connective tissue disease
Systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay for symptomatic or progressive interstitial disease
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab in refractory or relapsing disease
Supportive oxygen and pulmonary rehabilitation for breathlessness
Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests including transfer factor and interval imaging
Maintain surveillance for progression to fibrosis or transformation to pulmonary lymphoma
Refer to respiratory medicine and relevant specialties for multidisciplinary care
